title: How Advertising Grew Over Time

pages.text: Advertising has a very long history. People used it in ancient times. Egyptians used papyrus to make sales messages. Walls and rocks were also painted with ads. Today, we can still see old rock art paintings in Asia, Africa, and South America.

pages.text: In ancient China, people used oral messages and signs to sell items. Merchants used bamboo flutes to sell candy. They also used paper posters and inked plates. One old plate from the Song dynasty used a rabbit logo for a needle shop.
pages.caption: Bronze plate for printing an advertisement for the Liu family needle shop at Jinan, Song dynasty China. It is considered the world's earliest identified printed advertising medium.

pages.text: In the Middle Ages in Europe, many people could not read. Workers used pictures on signs instead of words. A boot meant a cobbler, and a horseshoe meant a blacksmith. Town criers also walked around to announce where fruit and vegetables were sold.

Modern advertising began with newspapers and magazines. The first weekly gazettes appeared in Europe in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Newspapers carried ads to help pay for printing costs. Early ads promoted books and medicines.

In the nineteenth century, advertising grew fast in the United States. Volney B. Palmer opened the first ad agency in Philadelphia. He bought newspaper space and resold it. Later agencies began to create complete ad campaigns with memorable slogans.

pages.text: In the twentieth century, new technologies changed advertising. Radio, television, and mobile devices brought ads to many people. Psychologists also helped advertisers understand how people think. Today, ads are a big part of the global economy.

The history of advertising dates back to ancient civilizations, where merchants used various methods to reach buyers. Egyptians utilized papyrus for sales messages, while wall paintings and rock art were common across Asia, Africa, and South America, with traditions dating back thousands of years.

pages.text: Ancient China recorded early forms of advertising through oral announcements, signboards, and printed papers. A copper printing plate from the Song dynasty, featuring a rabbit logo for a needle shop, is considered the world's earliest identified printed advertising medium.

pages.text: During the Middle Ages in Europe, widespread illiteracy led tradespeople to use symbols rather than words on their signs. A boot represented a cobbler, and a horseshoe stood for a blacksmith. Meanwhile, town criers walked through city streets to announce where goods were available.

Modern advertising began to develop with the introduction of newspapers and magazines in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. These publications carried advertisements to offset printing and distribution costs, initially promoting books and medicines before expanding to a wider variety of products.

In the nineteenth century, the growth of industrialization in the United States created a massive supply of manufactured goods. To find consumers for these products, companies turned to mass marketing. Advertising agencies emerged, transitioning from simple space brokers to firms that planned complete advertising campaigns.

pages.text: As the twentieth century progressed, new media like radio and television transformed the industry. Psychologists applied behavioral theories to advertising, focusing on basic human emotions and suggestions. American agencies also expanded globally, establishing a worldwide presence to support large manufacturing companies.

Tracing its origins to antiquity, advertising has long served commercial and political functions. Early manifestations included Egyptian papyrus notices, urban displays in Pompeii, and rock art traditions across Asia, Africa, and South America that originated millennia ago.

pages.text: Early commercial communication in China combined oral promotion with calligraphic signboards and printed media. Notably, a copper printing plate from the Song dynasty featuring a distinct rabbit trademark represents the earliest known printed advertising medium.
pages.caption: Bronze plate for printing an advertisement for the Liu family needle shop at Jinan, Song dynasty China. It is considered the world's earliest identified printed advertising medium.

pages.text: Amid medieval European urbanization and widespread illiteracy, merchants relied on pictorial trade insignia instead of text. Concurrently, itinerant town criers announced merchant locations, a practice documented in contemporary poetry such as Les Crieries de Paris.

The advent of periodicals in sixteenth- and seventeenth-century Europe catalyzed modern advertising structures. Newspapers incorporated commercial notices to subsidize production expenses, progressively broadening their scope beyond early book promotions and quack remedies.

Nineteenth-century industrial expansion in the United States necessitated mass marketing strategies to absorb surplus manufactured output. Consequently, advertising agencies evolved from rudimentary space brokering into comprehensive firms executing complex promotional campaigns.

pages.text: Twentieth-century technological innovations, coupled with the integration of applied psychological theory, fundamentally transformed commercial persuasion. As domestic markets matured, prominent agencies pursued international expansion alongside industrial conglomerates, embedding advertising deeply within global capitalist economies.

The history of advertising dates back to ancient civilizations, where merchants used various methods to reach buyers. Egyptians utilized papyrus for sales messages, while wall paintings and rock art were common across Asia, Africa, and South America, with traditions dating back thousands of years.
